$comment: Halal Scanner knowledge base. Every entry is reviewed:false until a qualified person reviews it with the founder. Do not set reviewed:true without that review. References describe where an ingredient comes from; they are not religious rulings.

entries.name: Pork and pig products
entries.shortReason: Comes from pigs, which are not halal.
entries.explanation: Pork and anything made from pigs (bacon, ham, gammon, etc.) is not halal according to all major schools of thought.

entries.name: Bacon / ham / pork flavouring
entries.shortReason: Often artificial, but it can contain real pork. Check with the manufacturer.
entries.explanation: Bacon, ham or pork "flavour" is often made without meat, but some flavourings contain real pork extract or fat. The label alone usually cannot tell you which.

entries.name: Lard (pork fat)
entries.shortReason: Fat from pigs, which is not halal.
entries.explanation: Lard is rendered pig fat. It is used in pastry, biscuits and some bread. It is not halal.

entries.name: Blood
entries.shortReason: Blood is not permitted to be eaten in Islam.
entries.explanation: Flowing blood is explicitly prohibited in the Quran. Products containing blood or blood plasma are not halal.

entries.name: Alcohol (ethanol, E1510)
entries.shortReason: Contains alcohol.
entries.explanation: Ethanol is the intoxicating alcohol in drinks. It is also used as a solvent or carrier in flavourings. Products listing alcohol as an ingredient are treated as not halal by the default profile.

entries.name: Wine, beer and spirits
entries.shortReason: An alcoholic drink is listed as an ingredient.
entries.explanation: Wine, beer and spirits are intoxicating drinks. When listed as an ingredient (for example in sauces, desserts or chocolates) the default profile treats the product as not halal.

entries.name: Alcohol-free beer or wine
entries.shortReason: "Alcohol-free" drinks can still contain a small amount of alcohol (up to about 0.5%).
entries.explanation: Beer and wine labelled "alcohol-free" or "non-alcoholic" are usually made by removing alcohol after fermentation and may still contain a trace. Scholars differ on these products.

entries.name: Rum / brandy / wine flavouring
entries.shortReason: May be made from or carried in alcohol; may also be artificial.
entries.explanation: Flavourings named after alcoholic drinks can be artificial, but some are made from the drink itself or dissolved in alcohol. Check with the manufacturer.

entries.name: Wine vinegar
entries.shortReason: Vinegar made from wine. Many scholars accept it; others avoid it.
entries.explanation: Wine vinegar is made by letting wine turn into vinegar. Many scholars consider it halal because the alcohol has been transformed; others avoid it, especially if it was made deliberately from wine. Scholars differ.

entries.name: Vanilla extract
entries.shortReason: Usually made with alcohol as a solvent; scholars differ on this.
entries.explanation: Vanilla extract is normally made by soaking vanilla beans in alcohol (often around 35%). Scholars differ on small amounts of alcohol used in processing.

entries.name: Meat (slaughter method not stated)
origins: animals that may not be halal-slaughtered
entries.shortReason: Meat must come from a halal-slaughtered animal; the label does not say.
entries.explanation: Meat from permitted animals is halal only if the animal was slaughtered in the Islamic way. Unless the product is halal-certified, this cannot be confirmed from the ingredient list.

qualifiers.reason: Label says the meat is halal. Check the certification logo.

entries.name: Animal fat
entries.shortReason: Fat from animals that may not be halal-slaughtered, or may be pork.
entries.explanation: Animal fat can come from pigs or from animals not slaughtered in the Islamic way. Unless the source and slaughter are confirmed, it is doubtful.

qualifiers.reason: Label says the fat is from pork.
Label says the fat is halal. Check the certification logo.

entries.name: Gelatin (E441)
entries.shortReason: Usually made from pork or non-halal beef; the source is not stated.
entries.explanation: Gelatin is made from animal skin and bones. Most gelatin worldwide comes from pigs; beef gelatin is halal only if the animal was halal-slaughtered; fish gelatin is generally accepted. Sweets, marshmallows, yoghurts and capsules often contain it.

qualifiers.reason: Label says the gelatin is from fish, which is generally accepted.
Label says the gelatin is from pork.
Beef gelatin is halal only if the animal was halal-slaughtered. Check for certification.
Label says the gelatin is halal. Check the certification logo.

entries.explanation: Collagen is extracted from animal skin and bones, often from pigs or cattle, sometimes from fish.

entries.name: Carmine / cochineal (E120)
entries.shortReason: Red colour made from crushed insects; scholars differ on it.
entries.explanation: Carmine (E120) is a red colour made from dried cochineal insects. Some schools consider insects impermissible to eat; others permit it. Found in red sweets, yoghurts and drinks.

entries.name: Shellac (E904)
entries.shortReason: Glaze made from a resin secreted by lac insects; scholars differ on it.
entries.explanation: Shellac (E904) is a shiny coating made from a resin secreted by the lac insect. It is used on sweets, chocolates and fruit. Many scholars permit it because it is a secretion; some avoid it.

entries.shortReason: Can be made from plant oils or animal fat; the source is not stated.
entries.explanation: Glycerol (E422) is made from fats and oils. It is often from vegetable oils, but it can come from animal fat including pork, or be made synthetically.

entries.name: L-cysteine / L-cystine (E920, E921)
entries.shortReason: Can be made from feathers, pig bristles or human hair; the source is not stated.
entries.explanation: L-cysteine (E920) is a flour treatment agent used in some bread and baked goods. It can be extracted from duck feathers, pig bristles or human hair, or made by fermentation.

qualifiers.reason: Label says it is synthetic or made by fermentation.

entries.name: Natural flavouring
entries.shortReason: Source is not stated. Natural flavourings can be animal-derived or carried in alcohol.
entries.explanation: "Natural flavouring" can come from plants or animals, and flavourings are often dissolved in alcohol. Without more detail from the manufacturer, the source cannot be confirmed.

qualifiers.reason: Label says the flavouring is halal. Check the certification logo.

entries.name: Enzymes
entries.shortReason: Enzymes can come from animals, including pigs; the source is not stated.
entries.explanation: Enzymes are used in cheese, bread and many processed foods. Many are made by microbes, but some come from animals, including pigs.

qualifiers.reason: Label says the enzyme is microbial or plant-based.
Label says the enzyme is from pork.

entries.name: Pepsin / lipase / trypsin
entries.shortReason: Often taken from pigs or calves; the source is not stated.
entries.explanation: Pepsin, lipase, trypsin and pancreatin are digestive enzymes. Commercial pepsin and pancreatin are usually from pigs; lipase can be animal or microbial.

qualifiers.reason: Label says the enzyme is microbial or plant-based.
Label says the enzyme is from pork.

entries.name: Rennet
entries.shortReason: Animal rennet comes from calves that may not be halal-slaughtered; the source is not stated.
entries.explanation: Rennet is used to make cheese. Animal rennet is taken from the stomach of calves (sometimes pigs). Microbial and vegetable rennet are widely accepted.

qualifiers.reason: Label says the rennet is microbial or plant-based.
Label says the rennet is from pork.
Label says the rennet is halal. Check the certification logo.

entries.name: Whey
entries.shortReason: A by-product of cheese-making, which may use animal rennet.
entries.explanation: Whey is left over from making cheese. If the cheese was made with animal rennet from a non-halal source, some scholars consider the whey doubtful; others permit it. Scholars differ.

qualifiers.reason: Label says the rennet used is microbial or plant-based.
Label says the whey is halal. Check the certification logo.

entries.name: Cheese
origins: milk with animal or microbial rennet
entries.shortReason: Cheese may be made with animal rennet; the rennet type is not stated.
entries.explanation: Many cheeses are made with animal rennet from calves that may not be halal-slaughtered. Cheese made with microbial or vegetable rennet (often marked "suitable for vegetarians") is widely accepted. Parmesan and Grana Padano are traditionally made with animal rennet.

qualifiers.reason: Label says the rennet used is microbial or plant-based.
Label says the cheese is halal. Check the certification logo.

entries.name: Shellfish and non-fish seafood
entries.shortReason: Most scholars consider seafood halal, but the Hanafi school differs on many non-fish sea creatures.
entries.explanation: The majority of scholars consider all seafood halal. In the Hanafi school, only fish is clearly permitted and scholars differ on prawns and shrimp; other shellfish are generally avoided. Shown as doubtful in the default conservative profile.
